paragraphs: When the headteacher of a secondary school in the north of England announced that phones would be banned during the school day, many students were furious. "How will my parents contact me?" asked one. "It's like going back to the Stone Age," complained another.

The rule was simple. Students could bring their phones, but they had to switch them off and lock them in a special pouch when they arrived. The pouches could only be opened at the end of the day. In an emergency, parents could call the school office, as they did in the past.

The first weeks were difficult. Some students tried to hide a second phone, and teachers had to deal with complaints every morning. But slowly, things changed. At lunchtime, the playground became noisier: instead of looking at screens, students were talking, playing football and even playing cards.

A year later, the school published some results. There were fewer fights and fewer cases of online bullying during school hours. Teachers said that students concentrated better in class, and exam results improved slightly. However, the head admitted that it was impossible to know if the phone ban was the only reason.

Not everyone is convinced. Some experts argue that schools should teach young people to use technology responsibly, not simply take it away. Phones can also be useful in lessons, for example to look up information or record a project.

Interestingly, many students changed their minds. "I hated it at first," says Maya, who is fifteen. "Now I actually like having a break from my phone. I don't feel I have to answer every message immediately."
